ai.definition: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic systems that are designed to be secure against both classical and quantum computers. These protocols aim to replace current public-key cryptography algorithms which could become vulnerable to attacks by quantum computers.
ai.howItWorks: PQC employs advanced mathematical problems, such as lattice-based cryptography, code-based cryptography, multivariate polynomial cryptography, hash-based signatures, and isogeny-based cryptography, to create secure encryption methods that are resistant to both classical and quantum computing threats. These algorithms leverage the computational complexity of these problems which are believed to be intractable for quantum computers.
ai.problemSolved: PQC addresses the security threat posed by future quantum computers, which could break many current cryptographic systems based on factoring large integers or discrete logarithms.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing and testing new algorithms that can resist attacks from both classical and quantum computers. This includes rigorous mathematical analysis to ensure the robustness of the protocols against various types of attacks.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for PQC involves extensive computational modeling, simulation, and testing on classical computers before deployment. It also requires collaboration between mathematicians, computer scientists, and cryptographers to develop and validate new cryptographic schemes.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of algorithm development, rigorous security analysis, and extensive testing. The cost can be high due to the need for robust validation against quantum attacks, which may require significant computational resources.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: PQC is currently in a research and specification phase with some standards being developed but not widely deployed yet.
ai.regulation: There are no specific regulations governing PQC at this stage. However, as these technologies mature, regulatory bodies may develop guidelines or standards to ensure their safe and effective use.
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for undiscovered vulnerabilities in new algorithms, the complexity of transitioning from current cryptographic systems, and the possibility that quantum computers could be developed faster than expected, rendering existing PQC solutions ineffective.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently speculative as there are no widely adopted commercial implementations. However, as quantum computing advances, the potential market for PQC could become significant.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on refining and standardizing PQC algorithms, improving efficiency, and ensuring interoperability with existing cryptographic systems.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Overall, the operational power requirements are moderate compared to quantum computing but can be higher during development stages.

glossary.def: Cryptography designed to be secure against both classical and quantum computers.
A type of PQC that uses the mathematical structure of lattices for security.
A computing device that utilizes quantum mechanics to perform operations on data, potentially much faster than classical computers.

subsystems.name: Key-encapsulation mechanism
subsystems.role: establishes a shared secret between two parties, replacing the role of Diffie–Hellman or RSA key transport.
parts: lattice arithmetic in a polynomial ring

subsystems.name: Digital signature scheme
subsystems.role: authenticates data, software and website certificates.
parts: lattice signatures for speed and small keys
hash-based signatures for very conservative security

subsystems.name: Symmetric primitives
subsystems.role: the bulk-encryption and hashing layer that quantum search algorithms only weaken, not break.

subsystems.name: Protocol integration
subsystems.role: carries the new algorithms through the standards real systems use.
parts: larger public keys and signatures (roughly 1–3 kB, tens of kB for some hash-based signatures)

subsystems.name: Implementation layer
subsystems.role: runs the maths safely on real hardware, including small embedded devices.

subsystems.name: Migration and agility tooling
subsystems.role: finds where old cryptography is used and swaps it out without breaking systems.

buildSteps.title: Pick the hard problem
buildSteps.detail: Designers choose a mathematical problem believed to resist both classical and quantum attack — most standards use the hardness of finding short vectors in high-dimensional lattices, while others use error-correcting codes or hash functions.

buildSteps.title: Choose parameters
buildSteps.detail: Key sizes, ring dimensions and error distributions are tuned so that the best known attacks need impractical effort, while keys and ciphertexts stay small enough for real networks.

buildSteps.title: Implement in constant time
buildSteps.detail: The algorithm is coded so that its running time and memory access pattern never depend on secret values; otherwise timing and cache attacks leak the key regardless of the maths.

buildSteps.title: Test and verify
buildSteps.detail: Implementations are checked against known-answer test vectors, fuzzed, formally verified where possible, and probed with side-channel measurement to confirm no secret-dependent leakage.

buildSteps.title: Standardise
buildSteps.detail: National standards bodies and the IETF turn the design into fixed specifications — NIST published its first post-quantum standards (covering key encapsulation and two signature schemes) in August 2024, with a code-based backup selected later.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into protocols
buildSteps.detail: Libraries such as OpenSSL, BoringSSL and others add the primitives, and protocol drafts define hybrid handshakes that combine a classical and a post-quantum exchange so the connection stays safe if either one falls.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and migrate
buildSteps.detail: Operators roll out hybrid key exchange first because it needs no new certificates, then move to post-quantum signatures, dual certificates and longer-term deprecation of RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.

prerequisites.tech: Quantum computers running Shor's algorithm at cryptographically relevant scale
prerequisites.why: no such machine exists; the threat today is 'harvest now, decrypt later', where encrypted traffic is stored for future decryption.

prerequisites.tech: Lattice and coding problems that resist attack
prerequisites.why: they are the security assumption, and while decades of cryptanalysis have not broken them, confidence rests on the absence of an attack rather than a proof.
new maths means new leakage paths; immature code can be broken by measurement rather than by mathematics.
key exchange is standardised and shipping, but post-quantum certificate chains, code signing and firmware signing standards are still settling.

prerequisites.tech: Capacity for much larger keys and signatures
prerequisites.why: post-quantum artefacts do not fit some constrained network protocols, smart cards and firmware images without redesign or fragmentation handling.

pathway.milestone: hybrid post-quantum key exchange in mainstream browsers, cloud providers and messaging apps
pathway.unlocks: protection against store-now-decrypt-later for ordinary web and chat traffic, with classical security retained as a fallback.

pathway.milestone: post-quantum signatures in TLS certificates, code signing and firmware updates
pathway.unlocks: end-to-end quantum-resistant authentication, and removal of the last RSA and elliptic-curve dependencies in many stacks.

pathway.milestone: cryptographic inventory, agility and automated rotation across enterprise and industrial systems
pathway.unlocks: the ability to replace an algorithm once, quickly, if a weakness is found — the main lesson of the migration.

pathway.milestone: deprecation of RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, alongside niche quantum key distribution for high-value links
pathway.unlocks: a cryptographic base that survives the arrival of large-scale quantum computers, rather than being rebuilt after it.
